extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a prior art reference qualifies as anticipatory or otherwise usable against claims (enablement, operability, availability, drawings, plant material, tax strategies, etc.) during patent examination and rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102/103/112.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An assertedly anticipating reference must provide an enabling disclosure of the desired subject matter; mere naming or description is insufficient if it cannot be produced without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of ordinary skill must be able to make or practice the claimed invention from the reference without undue experimentation (Elan Pharm. v. Mayo; In re Hoeksema). The reference is presumed operable until applicant rebuts with facts. If a process to make the compound was developed after the date of invention, mere naming in a reference is insufficient. Applicant must present evidence that a process for making was not known or operable at the relevant time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of unsuccessful attempts shows inoperability
rubrics_metrics.description: If attempts to prepare the compound disclosed in a reference were unsuccessful before the date of invention, that evidence can show the reference is inoperative (non-enabling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of unsuccessful prior attempts (In re Wiggins) can overcome a rejection. By contrast, mere absence of evidence that the author synthesized the compound does not, by itself, overcome operability when other patents show methods were known (In re Donohue). Court distinctions (Wiggins vs Donohue vs Hoeksema) illustrate that experimental failure evidence can be dispositive, while an author's non-attempt is not necessarily material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of secondary evidence to show enabling disclosure for 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: A 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection can be made even if the primary reference does not itself teach how to practice the invention, by citing secondary evidence (other patents/publications) to show public possession of methods of making/using.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reference teaches every claimed element, other patents/publications may be cited to demonstrate that the method of making/using was publicly available (In re Donohue). See MPEP § 2131.01 for procedures on using secondary references to show the primary contains an enabling disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-enabling references can still be used for obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-enabling reference may qualify as prior art for determining obviousness even if it would not anticipate under 102 because it is inoperative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held that an inoperative reference can be relied upon in a 103 obviousness analysis (Beckman Instruments v. LKB Produkter; Symbol Techs. v. Opticon). Examiners should consider such references when evaluating obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: One of ordinary skill must be able to make/synthesize
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a process for making the compound is not developed until after the date of invention, the mere naming of a compound in a reference cannot constitute a description (i.e., must be reproducible by one of ordinary skill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference is presumed operable until applicant rebuts (In re Sasse). Applicant bears burden to provide evidence that a process for making the compound was not available or that undue experimentation would be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictures/drawings can constitute enabling disclosure for apparatus/articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures and drawings may be sufficiently enabling to put the public in possession of the article pictured and therefore can anticipate claims to that article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The picture must show all claimed structural features and how they are put together (Jockmus v. Leviton). Origin of drawing is immaterial. When the reference is a patent, unintended or unexplained features in drawings may still be relied upon. See MPEP § 2125 / § 2121.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility not required in reference for anticipation of compound claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute anticipatory prior art for an old compound, a reference must identically disclose the compound, but it need not disclose a utility for the compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (In re Schoenwald; Impax Labs v. Aventis) state that proof of efficacy/utility is not required for a reference to anticipate a claim to an old compound; it suffices that the compound and its making are taught by the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant claims: ability to grow and reproduce the plant
rubrics_metrics.description: For plant claims, the reference (combined with prior art knowledge) must enable one of ordinary skill to reproduce the plant (grow/cultivate) without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographs alone may be insufficient if information like grafting/asexual reproduction is absent (In re LeGrice). Commercial availability (e.g., seeds) that permit reproduction can make the plant publicly possessed (Ex parte Thomson). Foreign sale plus publication and the ability to asexually reproduce without undue experimentation can create a 102(b) statutory bar (In re Elsner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents relevant for all they contain (nonpreferred/alternative embodiments are prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of patents as references is not limited to what patentees describe as their own invention; nonpreferred embodiments and alternatives disclosed may constitute prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference may be relied upon for all it would have reasonably suggested to one of ordinary skill, including nonpreferred embodiments. Disclosure of alternatives does not amount to teaching away unless the reference criticizes or discourages those alternatives (In re Heck; Merck v. Biocraft; In re Gurley; In re Fulton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Later factual references may be used to show universal facts (limited exception to critical date rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under certain circumstances, factual references that postdate the claimed invention may be used to show universal facts (e.g., characteristics of a material, that undue experimentation would have been required) even though they do not antedate the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include showing that undue experimentation would have been required (In re Corneil), that a parameter was or was not critical (In re Rainer), or that the invention lacked utility (In re Langer). However, later references cannot be used to determine whether the application satisfied 35 U.S.C. 112 enablement or written description (In re Koller). See cited cases for limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax strategies treated as prior art (AIA §14)
rubrics_metrics.description: For novelty/nonobviousness under 35 U.S.C. 102/103, any tax strategy (reducing/avoiding/deferring tax liability) shall be deemed insufficient to differentiate a claimed invention from the prior art; tax strategy limitations are treated as being within the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two exclusions: (1) parts solely for preparing tax returns or filing-related software are not covered; (2) financial management inventions severable from tax strategy are not covered. Examiners should: (1) construe claim (MPEP §2111); (2) analyze 35 U.S.C. 100/112 compliance; (3) identify tax-strategy limitations and note exclusions; (4) evaluate claim under 102/103 treating tax strategy limits as prior art (form para 7.06 may indicate tax strategy limitation). Computer-implemented methods that are novel and non-obvious remain patentable unless the only novel aspect is the tax strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings as prior art: evaluate disclosure, not scale/proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings and pictures can anticipate claims if they clearly show the structure claimed; proportions in drawings not to scale are not evidence of actual proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drawings are not stated to be to scale and dimensions are silent, measurements of drawings are of little value (Hockerson-Halberstadt v. Avia). Evaluate what the drawings and accompanying description would reasonably teach to one of ordinary skill. Examples (In re Mraz, In re Aslanian, In re Wright) show reliance on drawings plus description.

rubrics_metrics.name: The name 'patent' alone does not make a document prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A foreign document labeled a 'patent' is not necessarily available as a prior art patent under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)/(b); availability depends on substance of rights conferred and public accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secret patents (insufficiently accessible) are not available as prior art under 102(a)/(b) until publicly available, though they may be usable under 102(d) as of grant date. Accessibility (e.g., laid open for inspection or disseminated) determines availability. See In re Ekenstam, In re Carlson, In re Kathawala.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date foreign patent is effective as a reference
rubrics_metrics.description: The date a foreign patent is effective as a reference is usually the date patent rights are formally awarded (the date the sovereign bestows patent rights), subject to exceptions for secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Monks. MPEP § 901.05 provides tabular summaries for dates of patenting in many foreign jurisdictions; examiners should confirm availability dates by reviewing copies of the documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of disclosure when using a document as a 'patent' (not a 'publication')
rubrics_metrics.description: When a document is applied as a patent (rather than a printed publication), examiners may rely on unclaimed details in the patent specification that relate to the patented claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if certain matter was canceled from claims, the specification's disclosed details germane to the claimed subject matter can be used in a 102(a)/(b)/(d) rejection (Ex parte Ovist; In re Kathawala). However, matter canceled from the application file that did not issue cannot be relied on in a 102(e) rejection (see relevant cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandoned applications and availability as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: An abandoned application is evidence of prior art only when it has been appropriately disclosed to the public (e.g., referenced in another patent/publication or voluntarily disclosed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An abandoned application becomes available as of the date the public gains access to it (Lee Pharmaceutical v. Kreps). Subject matter of an abandoned application incorporated by reference in a published patent/application may be relied on in a 102(e) rejection based on that published patent/application. See MPEP §§ 2136.02-03 and 901.02 for procedural details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laid-open foreign applications and published U.S. applications as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign 'laid open' applications may constitute printed publications if made available for public inspection; U.S. published applications are preserved only in specified circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessibility and reproducibility determine 'printed publication' status (In re Wyer). Laid-open applications that were made available, microfilmed, or distributed in reproducible form have been held to be publications. Examiners should confirm publication/availability dates by reviewing copies. Pending U.S. applications are confidential except for published applications, reissues, or applications opened for inspection per 37 CFR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pending/copending U.S. applications and provisional rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending U.S. applications are generally confidential; however, copending applications that share inventors/assignees may give rise to provisional double-patenting or 102/103 provisional rejections when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims in copending applications are not independent or distinct, provisional double patenting rejections are made (MPEP §§ 706.02(a), 804, 2136). If copending applications differ by at least one inventor and one application would render the other obvious, make provisional 102(e) or 103 rejections where appropriate. See MPEP for procedural instructions about relying on U.S. application publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication standard (accessibility to the public)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is a 'printed publication' if it has been disseminated or otherwise made available such that persons interested and ordinarily skilled in the art, exercising reasonable diligence, can locate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The concept emphasizes probability of dissemination and public accessibility given modern reproduction/duplication technologies (In re Wyer; I.C.E. Corp. v. Armco). Lack of proof of public accessibility (e.g., undated mailer or post-filing distribution) defeats a 102(a) rejection (Carella v. Starlight Archery). Electronic publications are discussed in subsequent sections of the MPEP.
